news.title: Gold extends rebound as Nvidia CEO news lifts equities, dip-buying lifts bullion
Gold prices rebound strongly from last week’s rout as AI trade revs back to life
Gold's road back to $5,000: four big banks bet on recovery, but the Fed sets the pace
body: The banks' common message is that gold's direction in the coming months depends on the Fed, not on geopolitics. Throughout the Iran war, higher oil has fed rate-hike expectations and weighed on bullion. That makes upcoming US inflation data and the December Fed decision the key near-term drivers, with any signs of a peak in tightening likely to bring dip buyers back. Oil is the swing risk: BofA's stress case shows a renewed energy spike could keep gold under pressure well into 2027. Central bank buying, which Goldman estimates at around 60 tonnes a month, is the main floor beneath prices.
- The banks still believe in gold's recovery, but each target has been pushed back as the Fed keeps hiking, and the main question now is how long they'll have to wait.

Gold bounced back above $3,600 an ounce on Monday after a 9% slide last week took it to a 14-month low, and the major banks broadly agree on what comes next: a difficult few months while the Federal Reserve keeps hiking, followed by a recovery later in 2027. Where they differ is on how long the wait will be and how high the metal can go.

The common thread is the Fed. Expectations of further rate increases, high Treasury yields and a firm dollar have pushed gold down roughly 35% from its record near $5,600 in January. Throughout the Middle East conflict, gold has fallen rather than rallied on rising tension, because higher oil prices have fed inflation fears, rate hike expectations and higher yields. Every bank forecast below is, in effect, a call on when that pressure eases.

Goldman Sachs sees gold at $4,650 by the end of 2027, after trimming its target from $4,800 this month. Its economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December and again in March 2027, which the bank says will keep weighing on Western ETF demand. The support comes from official buyers: Goldman assumes central banks will buy around 60 tonnes a month from 2026 through 2028, against roughly 17 tonnes a month before 2022, and says that structural demand will help gold outperform silver. Once the Fed turns to rate cuts and Western investors return, it sees gold reclaiming $5,600 by the end of 2028.

UBS cut its year-end 2026 target to $4,500 last week but kept its forecast of $5,000 by the end of 2027, with $4,600 expected by mid-2027. In its 2027 outlook, it upgraded gold to attractive and recommended using pullbacks to add exposure, arguing that central bank buying, Chinese demand, resilient ETF holdings and concerns over government debt continue to support the metal. UBS described Monday's rebound as a stabilisation after last week's drop, helped by a softer dollar and bargain hunting, but expects volatility to stay high.

Bank of America is more cautious on timing. It expects gold to stay under pressure in the first half of 2027 and recover only in the second half, citing inconsistent physical buying, softening demand for gold-backed ETFs and its rate strategists' expectation of further Fed tightening in the first half of next year. BofA has also flagged a severe stress scenario, not its base case: if prolonged Middle East tensions push oil to $150 a barrel, it estimates gold would average just $3,500 in 2027.

Societe Generale has kept a 10% gold allocation in its multi-asset portfolio and recommends buying on dips, with a target of $5,000 by the end of 2027. It sees the US debt ceiling as the next catalyst. CIBC Capital Markets estimates the government could reach the $41.1 trillion limit as early as late February and that Congress may need to raise it by nearly $5 trillion to fund borrowing through the 2028 elections. SocGen expects another standoff to weigh on the dollar and revive concerns over US fiscal credibility, supporting gold. Its own $5,000 target has, however, been pushed back several times this year as rate hikes have taken their toll.

Taken together, the banks see gold ending 2027 somewhere between $4,650 and $5,000, which would mean gains of roughly 28% to 38% from around $3,630. All of them lean on the same pillars: central bank demand, an eventual peak in Fed tightening and, for some, US fiscal strain. The risk is in the timing. Each target has slipped as the Fed has stayed hawkish, and BofA's oil scenario shows how a renewed energy shock could push the recovery out further. For now, the question is less where gold ends up than how much more pain the Fed's hiking cycle has left to deliver.

news.title: BlackRock says markets overprice Fed hikes, sees two not three as energy shock fades
body: BlackRock's view runs against Monday's hawkish Fed commentary and against market pricing, so the October PCE data becomes a key test. A softer services reading would back BlackRock and could pull Fed pricing toward two hikes, supporting short-dated Treasuries and easing some pressure on the US dollar. For oil, BlackRock's case depends on the recent sharp fall in crude and fuel prices holding. A renewed rise in energy costs would undercut its view and strengthen the case for more Fed tightening. Its expectation of an ECB hike next month, with more depending on energy pass-through, points to tighter policy in Europe than the US for longer.
BlackRock thinks markets are pricing a Fed that will keep reacting to today's energy shock, when that shock is already reversing and will soon be pulling inflation down.

BlackRock believes markets have gone too far in pricing Federal Reserve rate hikes, arguing that a fading energy shock will bring headline US inflation down next year and allow the Fed to tighten less than investors expect.

In its weekly market commentary, the world's largest asset manager said it agrees with market expectations for a quarter-point Fed hike in December. But with pricing pointing to as many as three quarter-point increases over the next 12 months, BlackRock said that is overdone. It currently expects just one more hike in the first half of 2027.

At the centre of BlackRock's view is the energy shock from the Middle East conflict. It estimates the surge in energy prices added 1.5 percentage points to headline US inflation at its September peak. With Brent crude, gasoline and diesel prices all falling sharply this month, it expects that contribution to reverse, turning from a boost to inflation this year into a drag of 0.8 percentage points by the end of 2027. Lower fuel costs should also ease core inflation through cheaper transportation services.

BlackRock expects pressure from tariffs and the AI build-out to fade next year as well, though unevenly. It added that tighter financial conditions and uncertainty around AI spending could temper demand and hiring in 2027, further limiting price pressures.

BlackRock is not calling for an early end to tightening. The US economy is strong, the labour market is tight and wage growth of around 4% sits well above the 2% to 2.5% pace it sees as consistent with the Fed's target. That keeps core services inflation elevated, and BlackRock expects core inflation to stay closer to 3% than to the Fed's 2% goal. It also said the neutral interest rate may be higher than previously assumed, supporting further tightening even as energy relief arrives.

The contrast with Fed commentary is notable. On the same day, New York Fed President John Williams said he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if needed, and that the Fed would respond if inflation pressures do not ease. BlackRock's view implies a slower pace than that, with the October PCE inflation data, and especially services prices, a key test of which camp is right.

BlackRock also expects the European Central Bank to raise rates next month. It said the outlook beyond December depends on whether energy-driven price pressures continue feeding into underlying inflation, noting that earlier rises in natural gas prices are still reaching European consumers, prolonging inflation there relative to the US. The US, as a net energy exporter, is better placed to absorb the shock.
On growth, BlackRock sees the US expanding 2% to 2.5% this year and moderating but staying above 2% in 2027 as AI spending grows more slowly and the boost from tax cuts fades.

With two-year and 10-year Treasury yields reaching multi-decade highs this year, BlackRock said much of the long-anticipated structural rise in rates is now reflected in bond prices. It favours short- and medium-term Treasuries for income and protection against rate swings, and has strengthened its strategic overweight in inflation-linked bonds as a hedge against supply-driven inflation.

The commentary was written before Monday's sharp rebound in US stocks, after a week in which BlackRock noted solid Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's record IPO failed to lift AI sentiment and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory. If BlackRock is right that the market is over-pricing hikes, a repricing toward a gentler Fed path would favour short-dated bonds and ease some pressure on rate-sensitive equities.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6757 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: Goldman says AI's next test is proving the economics, not the technology
body: Goldman's focus on financing favours companies with strong balance sheets and reliable access to capital, which could widen the valuation gap between cash-rich hyperscalers and highly leveraged AI builders. Its view that agentic AI could push computing demand beyond user growth supports the chip, memory and power supply chain, consistent with its earlier note on AI spending broadening beyond Nvidia. Its expectation that permit and power constraints will shift where capacity is built, not reduce it, points to rising demand for sites with available energy, a theme relevant to utilities and energy markets. For newly listed AI names, the note's emphasis on execution suggests trading will stay sensitive to revenue updates.
Goldman's verdict: AI demand looks real, but the industry now has to prove it can pay for the computing that demand requires, and not every player will.

Goldman Sachs says the artificial intelligence debate is shifting from proving the technology to proving the economics, and that the gap between AI winners and laggards may widen as companies are forced to show the spending pays off.

In a note framed around last week's initial public offering of Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, the bank said the IPO comes at an important point in the AI cycle. The industry's focus is moving from training models to running them, a process known as inference, and to putting them to wider use. Anthropic listed on Nasdaq on November 19 after pricing at $83 a share and raising about $81 billion, the largest IPO on record. The shares opened sharply higher but fell about 8.5% the next day as a broad AI sell-off hit technology stocks.

Goldman said there are still returns to being at the frontier of AI. It noted that around 80% of Anthropic's usage is on its newest models, which suggests customers keep choosing greater capability. Models are still improving, both after their initial training and by using more computing power to reason before they answer. The bank added, however, that staying at the frontier requires continued heavy investment.

On competition from open-source models, Goldman said it is watching how competitive advantages evolve. Some open models are raising prices, which challenges the idea of an inevitable race to the bottom. Embedding AI into workflows, data and business processes can raise switching costs, while tailoring products to specific industries offers another potential source of pricing power.

The bank said evidence of real-world demand is building. Citing Anthropic figures, it said the number of customers spending at least $100,000 over the prior 12 months nearly doubled between the second and third quarters, and adoption now extends to more than half of the Fortune 500. Coding remains the largest use case, with cybersecurity growing and healthcare emerging. Agentic AI, which carries out multi-step tasks on its own, could add much more, and because each step consumes computing power, demand for computing could grow faster than the number of users.

The hardest question, in Goldman's view, is financing. Whether the data centres, chips and power behind frontier AI can be funded and built is increasingly a question of capital. The bank expects the winners to be companies with the balance sheet and access to capital to pay for computing power, and the ability to use it profitably. Owning infrastructure and using several types of chips may also reduce dependence on any single supplier.

Goldman said it is watching three things: execution, meaning whether better technology turns into revenue fast enough to justify continued investment; access to computing capacity, sites and cloud partnerships; and buildout limits such as permits, power and data centre restrictions. It expects those limits to delay capacity or shift where it is built rather than weaken demand.

The note's message cuts both ways for investors. Strong adoption data support the case that AI demand is real, but the scale of investment needed means returns are not guaranteed, and the volatile trading in AI stocks since Anthropic's debut shows how quickly sentiment can turn while that question remains open.

news.title: Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path
body: The openness to consecutive hikes adds upside risk to Fed pricing beyond December, with traders more likely to build in a follow-up move in early 2027. That should keep short-dated Treasury yields supported and give the US dollar a firmer floor, especially against currencies whose central banks are moving toward cuts. For equities, Williams set a high bar for market weakness to change his view, which limits hopes that renewed tech volatility would slow the Fed. Energy remains central to his inflation outlook, so any rise in oil prices would add weight to the case for a faster pace of hikes.
Williams' message to reporters was simple: December may only be the start, and only a much deeper slide in market confidence than the recent tech sell-off would make him rethink.

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Monday he would not rule out raising interest rates at consecutive meetings if needed, adding a sharper edge to a day of remarks in which he stressed that inflation remains too high.

Speaking to reporters after his speech at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York City, Williams said he has no particular timing in mind for further rate increases and has not pencilled in a path for policy. Incoming data will drive what the Fed does, he said, and officials will have to learn along the way. But he was clear that the range of outcomes is wide. "I'm not excluding options," Williams said, adding that he would not rule out moving at back-to-back meetings if that was what was needed. He also said the Fed will respond if inflation pressures do not ease.

That matters for how markets read the December 8-9 meeting. Investors broadly expect a quarter-point increase from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range, with more to come next year. The Fed last raised rates in September, so a December move would follow a pause. Williams' comments suggest a December hike need not be followed by a long wait, and that the pace of tightening could pick up if inflation data disappoint.

Williams also addressed the recent turbulence in stocks. He said he was not surprised by the market volatility and that swings in the tech sector have not upended his positive outlook for the economy. He did leave one caveat: if market sentiment darkened a lot, that could affect his view of the economy.

That caveat sets a high bar. The S&P 500 had slid more than 10% from its October record before Monday's Nvidia-led rebound, and Williams still described the outlook as positive. Read that way, only a deeper and more lasting drop in confidence, one that starts to hit spending and hiring, would be likely to make him rethink the case for tighter policy. Ordinary market swings, even sharp ones, appear unlikely to do so.

His press comments rounded out a consistent message across the day. In his prepared remarks, Williams said inflation is too high, risks are skewed to the upside and the Fed still has work to do, while forecasting inflation at 3.5% at the end of this year and back at the 2% target in 2028. In the question-and-answer session, he struck a more measured tone, describing recent inflation as driven by unusual factors and calling 2027 a year of lower inflation. His remarks to reporters made clear that the measured tone should not be mistaken for a reluctance to act.

The next tests are the economic data releases due before the December meeting. Hot readings would strengthen the case for a faster pace of hikes into early 2027, while softer data would give the Fed room to move more gradually.

news.title: ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028
body: The bigger story for currency markets is the policy divergence. The RBA is now widely expected to start easing in mid-2027, while the Fed is still on a hiking path, with a December increase broadly expected. A narrowing rate gap between the two would weigh on the Australian dollar against the US dollar over time. Short-dated Australian rates may see limited reaction, because markets had already priced a June cut as more likely than not after the jobs data. The effect is more likely to show up further out on the curve. Any upside surprise in quarterly inflation would test ANZ's call quickly and could prompt a sharp repricing back toward a later start to easing.
--- After five hikes this year, ANZ thinks the RBA will reverse course by mid-2027, though that depends on inflation cooling faster than the central bank itself expects.

ANZ now expects the Reserve Bank of Australia to begin cutting interest rates in June 2027, five months earlier than its previous forecast of November 2027, making it the first of Australia's big four banks to pencil in relief before the second half of next year.

In a research note released on Tuesday, ANZ Head of Australian Economics Adam Boyton set out a new easing path. The bank now sees a 25 basis point cut in June 2027, taking the cash rate from 4.85% to 4.60%, followed by a second cut in August 2027 to 4.35% and a third in February 2028 to 4.10%. Under its previous forecast, ANZ expected only two cuts, in November 2027 and February 2028.

The change comes less than a month after the RBA delivered its fifth rate increase of 2026 on November 3, lifting the cash rate to 4.85%, its highest level since 2008. The other three major banks currently expect the first cut in August 2027.

Boyton said three conditions need to play out over the next six months to justify a cut in the first half of next year: further deterioration in the labour market, an unwinding of excess demand across the economy and a moderation in underlying inflation. He said there is already early evidence pointing toward each of those developments.

The labour market is the most visible of the three. Employment fell sharply for a second straight month in October, pushing the unemployment rate up to 4.9%, a five-year high. That is above 4.75%, the RBA's estimate of the jobless rate consistent with stable inflation, a threshold that matters because it suggests the jobs market is no longer adding to price pressure.

Inflation is the harder test. The RBA's own forecasts, released after its November meeting, show inflation staying above 3% over the coming year and not returning to the top of its 2% to 3% target band until late 2027. For a June cut to happen, underlying price growth would need to slow faster than the central bank currently expects, or the RBA would need to be convinced that a weakening economy will finish the job.

ANZ's call also brings it closer to market pricing rather than ahead of it. After last week's jobs data, markets put the odds of a quarter-point cut at the June 2027 meeting at around 68%, rising to about 90% for August. Because the forecast still implies an extended hold from here, its main effect is on pricing further out along the yield curve rather than on expectations for the next few RBA meetings.

The key risks to the view run in both directions. A rebound in hiring or stubborn services inflation could push cuts back toward the second half of 2027, while a sharper slowdown could bring them forward again. Quarterly inflation and monthly jobs data over the next six months will decide which way the call breaks.

news.title: Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia
body: Goldman's framing favours the bottleneck parts of the AI supply chain, particularly memory makers, advanced packaging specialists and power infrastructure, over a single-stock bet on Nvidia. That is relevant for Asian equities, where memory and packaging exposure is concentrated in Korea and Taiwan. The view that neocloud lending now depends on milestones should ease some credit concerns around the sector, although it also implies slower, more conditional build-outs. The power angle ties AI spending to energy and utilities demand, a theme that is likely to keep electricity infrastructure in focus as data centre construction grows.
Goldman's message is that the AI build-out is bigger than any one company: even if Nvidia's share shrinks, the trillions keep flowing, just into more hands.

Goldman Sachs believes $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, and argues that a growing share of that spending is reaching companies beyond Nvidia, including memory makers, chip packaging specialists and power suppliers.

The bank's note was written before Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, when the company's leadership was still in doubt. That timing matters. Several of the risks it weighed, including uncertainty over Nvidia's product roadmap, have eased with Huang's return. Its central argument does not depend on who runs Nvidia, though: in Goldman's view, near-term demand for AI infrastructure remains intact.

On the supply side, Goldman said demand is outstripping supply across memory, server processors and chipmaking equipment. Nvidia sells far more than graphics processors, including networking gear, central processors, complete server systems and the software that ties them together. Even so, the bank noted that investment is increasingly reaching areas Nvidia does not supply, such as memory, advanced packaging, which covers how chips are assembled and connected, and power.

That leads to what may be the note's most useful framing for investors. Goldman said any loss of Nvidia market share would change who gets which slice of the AI pie, not the size of the pie. Supply constraints and long design cycles limit how quickly share can shift, but uncertainty over Nvidia's longer-term roadmap could help rival chip designers and their suppliers. The bank also flagged that if Nvidia's work on open-source models and enterprise tools slowed, closed-model developers could benefit at the expense of software firms that rely on fast open-source progress. Huang's return makes that scenario less likely in the near term.

Monday's market reaction offered a live test of the thesis. When Huang returned, memory makers and other AI suppliers rallied alongside Nvidia, consistent with Goldman's view that the AI spending wave lifts a broad supply chain rather than a single company.

For investors, the takeaway is less about Nvidia's leadership drama than about where AI capital is heading next. If Goldman is right that spending is broadening into memory, packaging and power, the bottlenecks in those areas may matter as much for returns as Nvidia's market share. The main risk to that view is a slowdown in AI investment itself, which would shrink the pie rather than reshuffle it.
